title: Insider Threat
summary: An insider threat is harm to an organisation caused by someone who already holds legitimate access, such as an employee, contractor, supplier or a partner account, rather than by an external attacker who must first break in. It is usually split into three motives: a malicious insider who intends harm, often acting shortly before resigning or after a dispute; a negligent insider who takes a shortcut, misconfigures a share or sends data to the wrong recipient; and a compromised insider, whose valid account or device an external attacker has taken over. The technical problem is that insider activity looks like normal business activity, because it uses approved tools, valid credentials and expected network paths, so signature and perimeter controls see very little. Detection leans on behavioural baselines, monitoring of privileged and bulk actions, data loss prevention, separation of duties and prompt offboarding. The common mistake is planning only for the malicious case and building a surveillance culture, while ignoring that most real incidents begin with an error or a phished account, and that excessive standing access turns an ordinary mistake into a serious one.

beginner.definition: An insider is someone who already has allowed access to your systems, such as an employee, a contractor or a supplier. An insider threat is harm that comes from that access being misused. The misuse can be on purpose, by accident or because an outsider stole the account. It is not always a person acting like a villain.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security tools look for strangers breaking in from outside. An insider already has a key, so alarms stay quiet. They can copy customer lists, delete backups or weaken a control slowly. An honest mistake, such as sharing a folder with the whole company, can leak private data just as badly. If you do not limit access, one careless click can do serious damage.
howItWorks: A person is given an account and permissions so they can do their job each day.
The organisation records what normal work looks like for that role, which is called a baseline.
Monitoring tools compare new activity with that baseline and flag sudden unusual behaviour.
Examples include copying large data sets, logging in at strange hours or touching files outside the role.
Controls such as least privilege, approval steps and fast removal of access reduce the damage.
Investigators then review the alerts carefully, because normal work can look suspicious too.
beginner.example: Imagine a hotel front desk at night. Staff have keys to the rooms, the safe and the storeroom, because they need them to help guests. A new worker copies the guest list onto a personal phone, thinking it will help tomorrow. A tired worker leaves the storeroom unlocked. A thief takes a uniform and a key card from a locker. In all three cases the hotel was not broken into; the keys were used. The desk stays safer when each key opens only what that shift needs, when copying the guest list needs approval, and when lost keys are cancelled at once.
takeaways: Insiders already have access, so perimeter tools often do not notice them.
Most insider incidents start with an accident or a stolen account, not with revenge.
Limit access to what the job needs, and remove it quickly when someone leaves.

objectives: Define insider threat and distinguish malicious, negligent and compromised insiders.
Explain why valid credentials and approved tools make insider activity hard to detect.
Describe how baselines and behavioural monitoring support detection of unusual activity.
Identify controls that reduce insider risk, including least privilege, separation of duties and prompt offboarding.
Discuss the balance between monitoring for real risk and respecting employee privacy.
